title: Client Conversation business-node assembly and keyed Chat snapshots
summary: The browser builds the conversation view through an assembly engine: business plugins register event definitions, view plugins register builders, and the client session class only feeds the engine a window of events.
firstReason: The fold from session events to conversation nodes is still needed, but it runs in the Go host, which renders the nodes as HTML fragments; the client-side engine and keyed React snapshots go away.

title: Client-Derived Presentation from Raw Session Tool Events
summary: Session history sent to the browser contains only raw persisted events; the client derives tool cards from the tool name, arguments and result, and the host does not run tool presenters while reading history.
firstReason: The rule that history reads stay free of the tool registry is kept, but the derivation moves to the Go host's rendering layer, which builds card HTML from the raw events.

title: Two-stage Composer and DraftEditor isolation
summary: Proposal (first stage built upstream): split the message composer into a session-owned draft model (text, attachments, submission) and per-view editor instances that own only DOM and caret state, as a mechanical extraction first and a behaviour change second.
firstReason: The split is kept and becomes natural: the Go host owns the draft and attachments per session, and the rich-text input is a small script island that owns only the caret and DOM. The two-step refactoring plan is upstream process.

title: Definition-owned grouping with generic Node/Group assembly
summary: Grouping chat content into expandable groups is owned by registered group definitions; the builder and assembler stay generic. All three display densities share one grouping result, so that switching density does not rebuild React component instances.
firstReason: The separation (business grouping rules apart from a generic assembler) is worth keeping in the Go view model. The instance-identity constraints exist only for React; server-rendered HTML computes groups in the host and renders them.

title: Initial draft content and structured reference restoration
summary: Starting a session can prefill the composer with a prompt, with an explicit rule for when a draft already exists (keep, replace or append). Drafts keep structured references (file, folder and session chips), and the initial content is in place before the input is first read.
firstReason: The prefill options and the rule that prefilling never sends are product behaviour to keep. The mechanism (input model objects, React mount order) is client-internal; in the Go UI the draft document lives in the rich-text island and the host supplies the initial content with the page.

title: Claimed commands as atomic composer chips
summary: A slash command the composer has recognised becomes one atomic chip node in the editor instead of styled text. Deleting the chip releases the command claim, and undo restores it.
firstReason: The chip replaced a text transform that looped inside the Lexical editor library. The behaviour (a recognised command is one unit, and the claim follows the document) should be kept; the editor is a JavaScript island whose library and node model the UI area chooses.

title: User-text candidate scheduling and Facts-driven refresh
summary: References inside user text (sessions, files, skills, commands) are recognised by registered rules. Each rule returns its nearest match from a position in the original text, and one loop resolves overlaps deterministically and reuses work when known facts change.
firstReason: The algorithm is pure logic and is worth keeping. In the Go UI it runs in the host when the message is rendered, so the incremental refresh that exists to avoid React re-rendering is unnecessary. Go string offsets are bytes, not UTF-16 units.

title: Exclusive Conversation matches
summary: A conversation node definition can claim an event exclusively for its target, so that a generic definition does not also render it. Two claims on one event are an error that names both.
firstReason: It prevents double rendering when a specific renderer and a generic one both match. A server-side renderer registry needs the same rule (the specific renderer wins, conflicts are errors), expressed as Go dispatch.

title: Draft attachments across Session switches
summary: A composer draft that has attachments keeps its session's scope alive without an event connection, so switching sessions and back keeps the attachments, running uploads and retry state. After a page reload the composer says the attachments were discarded instead of restoring them.
firstReason: The goal (a draft's attachments survive a session switch) stands. Because images and files are already uploaded to the host when added, the Go design can keep the draft's attachment list on the host, which would also survive a reload.

title: Durable rich-text quotes in the Web composer
summary: A selected transcript excerpt becomes an atomic quote node in the composer's rich-text editor. Drafts persist quote text and spans in a semantic snapshot, not raw editor state, so they survive reload, session switches and failed sends.
firstReason: Quoting stays a feature and the semantic draft snapshot is the right durable form. The editor is one of the JavaScript islands DH-ADR-3 allows, so the quote node is rebuilt inside that island and the React slot wiring around it goes away.

title: Frame-coalesced reasoning-chunk publication and browser stress validation
summary: Every live chunk of a streaming reply is folded into state at once, but the UI is redrawn at most once per browser animation frame; the durable settlement publishes immediately. An opt-in browser stress test validates it.
firstReason: The goal stands: a long reasoning stream must not cause one redraw per chunk. With HTML streamed over server-sent events (DH-ADR-3) the coalescing moves to the Go host, which should batch live updates to a bounded rate before sending them; the React publication mechanism does not exist.
